cards.front: Define imperfect competition and monopolistic competition. Compare the four market structures on the spectrum of competition.
cards.back:
Imperfect competition — any market that is not perfectly competitive, so firms have some power over their price. Monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly are all forms of imperfect competition.

Monopolistic competition — a market with many firms and low barriers to entry, where each firm sells a slightly different product. Hairdressers, cafés and takeaways in a town are typical examples. Where the Edexcel B specification lists imperfect competition alongside monopoly and oligopoly, it means monopolistic competition.

  • Perfect competition: very many small firms, no barriers to entry, identical products → no power over price: firms are price takers.
  • Monopolistic competition: many firms, low barriers, slightly different products → a little power over price.
  • Oligopoly: a few large firms dominate, high barriers, identical or branded products → considerable power, but each firm watches its rivals.
  • Monopoly: one firm, very high barriers, no close substitutes → high power: a price maker.

The further a market sits towards monopoly, the more market power each firm has: the ability to raise its price without losing all its customers.

cards.front: Define perfect competition. Sketch the market and the firm when demand has risen. What happens next, and where does the model fall short?
cards.back:
Perfect competition — a market with very many small firms selling homogeneous products, with perfect information and no barriers to entry or exit.

The market's demand and supply set the price, P1. Each firm is a price taker: a firm charging a penny more would sell nothing, so its demand curve is the horizontal line D=AR=MR=P1. It produces Q1, where MC cuts the price line.

  • Short run: P1 is above average cost C1 → the shaded rectangle is supernormal profit.
  • Entry: the profit signals an opportunity → new firms join, which is easy with no barriers → market supply rises → the price falls.
  • Long run: entry continues until the price equals the lowest average cost → each firm makes only normal profit.

Where it falls short: products are rarely identical, information is not perfect, entry is rarely free, and economies of scale mean firms are not all small. With every idea copied at once and profit competed away, firms also have little reason to innovate. It is a benchmark, not a description of real markets.

Right, the firm: cost and revenue on the vertical axis, a horizontal line D=AR=MR=P1, an MC=S curve and a U-shaped AC curve. The firm produces Q1, where MC meets the price line, at average cost C1, and the shaded rectangle between P1 and C1 is supernormal profit

cards.front: Sketch the market and the firm in perfect competition after new firms have entered. Why does supernormal profit disappear, and what happens if demand falls instead?
cards.back:
Market: new firms enter → supply shifts right from S1 to S2 → the price falls from P1 to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.

Firm: the new price is its horizontal demand curve, D=AR=MR=P2. It just touches the lowest point of AC, where MC also crosses, so the firm produces Q2 and the price P2 equals average cost C2.

  • Why the profit goes: supernormal profit signals an opportunity → with no barriers, new firms keep joining → market supply keeps rising → the price keeps falling until it equals the lowest average cost → each firm makes only normal profit, just enough to stay in the market.
  • If demand falls instead: the price falls below average cost → firms make losses → some leave → market supply falls → the price rises until normal profit returns.

In the long run, consumers pay a price equal to the lowest average cost. This is the price mechanism at work.

Right, the firm: cost and revenue on the vertical axis, a horizontal line D=AR=MR=P2 that just touches the lowest point of the U-shaped AC curve, where the MC=S curve also crosses, at output Q2. cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how does a firm's freedom to set its price change along the spectrum of competition, and which pricing strategies can it use?
cards.back:
• Perfect competition: firms take the market price → there is no pricing strategy to choose.
  • Monopolistic competition: a loyal customer base → the firm can charge a little more than rivals without losing every sale → but a large gap sends customers elsewhere, so prices stay close to rivals'.
  • Oligopoly: each firm's sales depend on what its rivals charge → a price cut is likely to be matched → firms avoid price wars, keep prices stable and often compete in other ways.
  • Monopoly: no close substitutes → the firm sets its own price → it can price above cost and keep supernormal profit, because barriers stop rivals entering.

Strategies: competitive pricing, close to rivals', is the norm where products are similar. Price skimming only works while a product has no close rivals. Predatory pricing needs a large firm that can afford losses for a while.

In an answer, name the market structure first, then explain what it means for the firm's freedom to set prices.

cards.front: Define non-price competition. In which market structures does it matter most, and how can it raise a firm's profit?
cards.back:
Non-price competition — winning customers through anything other than a lower price, such as quality, branding, advertising or where the product is sold.

It matters most in monopolistic competition and oligopoly, where firms have products to set apart and, in oligopoly, a price cut would simply be matched.

Methods: branding and advertising, quality and design, customer service, loyalty schemes, and convenience, such as location, opening hours or a good app.

Successful non-price competition → customers see fewer close substitutes → demand becomes more price inelastic → the firm can charge more without losing many sales → higher profit.

The catch: advertising and loyalty schemes are expensive, and rivals copy anything that works.

cards.front: Evaluate the claim that less competition in a market is always bad for consumers.
cards.back:
Why it can be bad:

  • Higher prices: fewer rivals → less pressure to cut prices → consumers pay more and buy less.
  • Less choice: fewer firms → fewer products to choose between → consumers lose out if the one on offer doesn't suit them.
  • Weaker pressure on quality: customers have nowhere else to go → less need to improve service or products → quality can slip.

Why it may not be:

  • Economies of scale: a large firm may have such low costs that it charges less than many small firms could, even with market power.
  • Use of profit: supernormal profit can pay for research and new products, so consumers may gain in the long run.
  • Contestability: if new firms could enter easily, even a dominant firm keeps its prices down to stop them.
  • Regulation: regulators can cap prices or block mergers where market power harms consumers.

Judgement: not always. It depends most on how easily new firms could enter and whether the dominant firm's lower costs and profits are passed on to consumers.

cards.front: Define barriers to entry and intellectual property rights. Name seven types of barrier to entry, with how each keeps new firms out.
cards.back:
Barriers to entry — anything that makes it hard or costly for a new firm to start selling in a market.

  • Product differentiation: the more customers see a product as unique, the fewer substitutes a newcomer can offer, so it has to spend heavily to win anyone over.
  • Branding: loyal customers keep buying even when a newcomer is cheaper, so an entrant must spend large sums on advertising, a sunk cost if it fails.
  • Start-up costs: a factory or a network of masts costs a fortune before the first sale, and lenders see a newcomer as risky.
  • Intellectual property rights — legal rights over ideas and creative work, such as patents, trademarks and copyright. A UK patent can stop others making or selling an invention for up to 20 years.
  • R&D and technology change: heavy R&D builds know-how newcomers cannot match quickly. But new technology can also knock barriers down, as online selling did for small retailers.
  • Legal barriers: licences, such as a taxi licence or a bank's authorisation, limit the number of firms or make entry slow and costly.
  • Anti-competitive practices: predatory pricing, exclusive dealing or refusing to supply shops that stock a rival. Competition law bans these when a dominant firm uses them.

cards.front: Define a contestable market. What are sunk costs and hit-and-run entry? How do firms already in a contestable market behave?
cards.back:
Contestable market — a market where barriers to entry and exit are low, meaning firms can easily and cheaply enter and leave the market.

Contestability is about the threat of new rivals, not the number of firms already there. A market with two firms can still be contestable if others could join quickly.

Sunk costs are money spent on entering that cannot be got back on exit, such as advertising or equipment with no resale value. Low sunk costs make hit-and-run entry possible: a firm joins to take a share of high profits and leaves when they fall.

  • Prices: high profits would attract entrants → firms keep prices close to average cost, called limit pricing → consumers pay less and firms earn close to normal profit.
  • Quality and costs: an entrant could win customers with a better or cheaper product → firms keep costs down and service up → consumers gain even with few firms.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how does the height of barriers to entry decide a market's structure, and what decides how long a barrier protects the firms inside?
cards.back:
• High barriers: new firms are kept out → a few firms or one firm supplies the market → oligopoly or monopoly → firms keep supernormal profit in the long run and can charge consumers more.
  • Low barriers: new firms enter whenever profits are high → many firms compete → monopolistic or near-perfect competition → profit is competed down to normal and prices fall towards average cost.

How much a barrier protects depends on:

  • How long it lasts: patents expire and brands can fade, so supernormal profit may only be temporary.
  • Technology: new ways of producing or selling can make an old barrier irrelevant.
  • The size of the entrant: a large firm from another market can afford start-up costs and advertising that would stop a small business.
  • Regulation: competition authorities can block mergers or practices that raise barriers on purpose.

cards.front: Define economies of scale. Build the chains: how do they affect the costs and prices of a large firm, its consumers and a new entrant? When do consumers not gain?
cards.back:
Economies of scale — the fall in long-run average cost that comes from producing on a larger scale.

Average cost falls until the minimum efficient scale (MES). The main types are purchasing (bulk discounts), technical (automated machinery), financial (cheaper borrowing) and marketing (one campaign spread over more units).

  • The large firm: output rises → average cost falls → it can cut prices and still make a profit, or keep prices and earn a higher margin.
  • Consumers: lower average cost is passed on → lower prices.
  • A new entrant: it starts small → its average cost is higher than established rivals' → it cannot match their prices without a loss, so economies of scale work as a barrier to entry.

Consumers may not gain when: a firm protected by barriers keeps the savings as profit; growth goes past the MES and diseconomies push costs back up; or the MES is a large share of total demand, so the market only has room for a few firms.

cards.front: One firm has 70% of a market. Evaluate whether it will be able to raise its prices well above its costs.
cards.back:
Why it may: a large share suggests high barriers, such as strong branding, high start-up costs or patents → rivals cannot enter to undercut it → it can charge more and keep supernormal profit.

Why it may not:

  • Contestability: if entry and exit are cheap, the threat of hit-and-run entry keeps its prices close to average cost, whatever its share.
  • Barriers fade: a patent expires or a brand weakens, so the power may be temporary.
  • Technology: a new way of producing or selling can let rivals get round an old barrier.
  • Large entrants: a big firm from another market can afford the start-up and advertising costs.
  • Regulation: competition authorities can act against practices that raise barriers on purpose.

Judgement: the market share alone does not answer it. Look for evidence on how easy entry is — start-up costs, patents, brand loyalty — before judging whether the firm can raise its prices. Competition and contestability are not the same thing.

cards.front: Define an oligopoly and a concentration ratio. State the formula for an n-firm concentration ratio, and give two limits of the measure.
cards.back:
Oligopoly — a market dominated by a few large, interdependent firms, protected by high barriers to entry.

Concentration ratio — the share of a market's total sales taken by its largest firms.

The higher the ratio, the more concentrated the market. A market is usually called an oligopoly when the top few firms hold most of it.

Limits:

  • It does not show how sales are shared among the top firms: a 4-firm ratio of 80% could be one giant and three small firms, or four equals.
  • It depends on how the market is drawn: a firm with a small share of national sales might dominate one town.

cards.front:
A city's taxi firms take £80m a year in fares. The five largest firms take £24m, £16m, £12m, £8m and £4m.

(a) Calculate the 2-firm and 4-firm concentration ratios. (b) What share is left for the rest of the market? (c) A second city's 4-firm ratio is also 75%, with each of its four largest firms at about 19%. Are the two markets the same?
cards.back:
(a)

  • 2-firm: (£24m + £16m) ÷ £80m × 100 = 50%
  • 4-firm: (£24m + £16m + £12m + £8m) ÷ £80m × 100 = £60m ÷ £80m × 100 = 75%

(b) 100% − 75% = 25% for every other taxi firm, the fifth largest included. Four firms share three quarters of the market, so it is concentrated, and each will watch what the other three charge.

(c) No. The ratios match, but in the first city the largest firm alone has 30% (£24m ÷ £80m), while in the second the four are roughly equal. A concentration ratio does not show how sales are shared among the top firms.

cards.front: Define interdependence. Sketch the kinked demand curve and use it to explain why prices in an oligopoly tend to stay stable. When does stability break down?
cards.back:
Interdependence — when each firm's sales and profit depend on what its rivals do, so it has to predict their reaction before it acts.

The kink sits at the current price, labelled Pcomp, and output Q.

  • If the firm raises its price: rivals don't follow → customers switch to them → demand above the kink is price elastic → revenue falls.
  • If it cuts its price: rivals match the cut → the firm gains few sales → demand below the kink is price inelastic → revenue falls.

Either way it loses, so it leaves its price where it is and uses non-price competition instead.

A second reason: the MR curve has a vertical gap at Q. Profit is maximised where MC = MR, so MC can rise or fall inside the gap with no change in the best price. Even a change in costs may leave prices unchanged.

Breakdown: a firm with much lower costs, or a new entrant, cuts prices to win market share → rivals follow in a price war → consumers gain for a while, every firm's revenue and profit fall, and weaker firms may leave.
cards.svgAlt: Kinked demand curve with cost and revenue on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. The demand curve D=AR is flatter above the kink, labelled price elastic demand, and steeper below it, labelled price inelastic demand. The kink sits at price Pcomp and quantity Q. The MR curve has a vertical gap at Q, and the MC=S curve passes through the gap. An AC curve gives average cost C at Q

cards.front:
Define tacit agreement. Two ferry operators on one crossing each choose a high or a low fare. Yearly profits (Operator A, Operator B) are:

  • Both high: £8m, £8m
  • A high, B low: £2m, £11m
  • A low, B high: £11m, £2m
  • Both low: £5m, £5m

What will each choose, and why does this tempt firms into a tacit agreement? Who gains and loses from one, and when is it likely to hold?
cards.back:
Tacit agreement — firms coordinating their prices or output without any formal or spoken agreement, for example by following a price leader.

The matrix: whatever B does, A earns more with the low fare (£11m beats £8m, and £5m beats £2m), and the same is true for B. So both choose low fares and earn £5m each, though both would earn £8m if they kept fares high. That is the pull towards an agreement.

An open agreement to fix prices, a cartel, is illegal in the UK. A tacit one has no meeting or contract, so it is much harder to prove, but the result can be the same.

  • Firms: prices stay above the competitive level → higher margins → supernormal profit.
  • Consumers: prices are higher than with real competition → they pay more and buy less → lower real incomes.

More likely to hold when: there are very few firms, so a price cut is easy to spot; products and costs are similar; barriers to entry are high; and demand is stable, since a downturn strengthens the pull to cut prices.

cards.front: Define price discrimination and its three degrees. What three conditions does third-degree price discrimination need? Sketch it for two groups of customers.
cards.back:
Price discrimination — charging different customers different prices for the same product, where the difference is not caused by a difference in cost.

  • First-degree: each customer pays the most they are willing to pay, as at an auction.
  • Second-degree: the price depends on how much is bought, such as bulk discounts.
  • Third-degree: different groups of customers pay different prices.

Conditions: market power, as a price taker cannot set prices; groups with different PED that the firm can tell apart; and separate markets, so low-price buyers cannot resell to high-price ones.

The diagram: the firm sets MC = MR in each sub-market. In the sub-market where demand is price inelastic it charges a high price, and in the one where demand is price elastic it charges a lower one. A gym might charge more for evening sessions, when people who work can only come then, than for weekday daytime ones.

The two shaded profit areas together are larger than the profit the firm would make charging one price across the combined market.
cards.svgAlt: Two panels with cost and revenue on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, sharing one horizontal AC=MC line at C. Left, the inelastic sub-market: a steep D=AR and MR, output Q where MR meets MC, a high price P and a shaded profit rectangle between P and C. Right, the elastic sub-market: a flatter D=AR and MR, output Q, a lower price P and a shaded profit rectangle

cards.front: Evaluate third-degree price discrimination. Who gains, who loses, and is it good or bad overall?
cards.back:
• The firm gains: each group pays closer to the most it is willing to pay → more consumer surplus becomes revenue → higher profit than with one single price.
  • Customers with inelastic demand lose: they are charged more than a single price → they lose consumer surplus.
  • Customers with elastic demand can gain: they are charged less → some can now afford the product at all.

Whether it is good or bad depends on:

  • Use of the extra profit: it may pay for investment, or keep a service running that would otherwise close, such as a lightly used rail route.
  • Who pays more: it is harder to defend if the high price falls on people on low incomes with no choice.
  • Use of capacity: cheap off-peak prices fill places that would otherwise be empty, at very little extra cost.

Judgement: the firm gains and customers with inelastic demand lose, so it is not good for everyone. It is easiest to defend where the low price brings in customers who would otherwise go without, and the extra profit keeps a service running.

cards.front: Define average cost (AC) and average revenue (AR), with the formula for each. How can profit be found from the averages?
cards.back:
Average cost (AC) — the cost of producing one unit, found by dividing total costs by output. AC = Total cost ÷ Quantity.

Average revenue (AR) — the revenue from each unit sold, found by dividing total revenue by output. AR = Total revenue ÷ Quantity.

If every unit sells for the same price, AR is simply the price. That is why a firm's demand curve is also its AR curve.

Profit is total revenue minus total cost. From the averages, it is profit per unit (AR − AC) times the number sold.
cards.formulaHtml: Profit=(AR−AC)×Quantity\text{Profit} = (\text{AR} - \text{AC}) \times \text{Quantity}Profit=(AR−AC)×Quantity

cards.front: Define marginal cost (MC) and marginal revenue (MR). Why is MR below the price for most firms? How do MC and MR link to contribution?
cards.back:
Marginal cost (MC) — the extra cost of producing one more unit.

Marginal revenue (MR) — the extra revenue from selling one more unit. MR = Change in total revenue ÷ Change in quantity.

MR below price: to sell more, most firms must cut the price, and the lower price applies to every unit, not just the extra one. So MR is below the price and falls faster than AR.

Contribution: fixed costs don't change when one more unit is made, so MC is all variable cost. MR − MC is the contribution of the extra unit, towards fixed costs and then profit.

  • MR above MC: a positive contribution → total contribution and profit rise → produce it.
  • MR below MC: a negative contribution → profit falls → don't.

So profit is highest where MC = MR. Unlike break-even analysis, where every unit makes the same contribution, here it shrinks with each unit because the price has to fall to sell more.
cards.formulaHtml: MC=Change in total costChange in quantity\text{MC} = \frac{\text{Change in total cost}}{\text{Change in quantity}}MC=Change in quantityChange in total cost​

cards.front:
A workshop builds custom bicycle frames. To sell more each week it must lower its price. Fixed costs are £300 a week.

  • Frames (Q): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
  • Price: £500, £450, £400, £350, £300, £240, £190
  • Total cost: £400, £470, £540, £660, £840, £1,080, £1,330

(a) Calculate MR and MC for the 4th and 5th frames, and find the profit-maximising output and price. (b) Show the maximum profit two ways. (c) What price would a revenue maximiser and a sales maximiser charge? (d) Profit per frame is highest at 3 frames. Why not make 3?
cards.back:
(a) TR at 3, 4 and 5 frames is £1,200, £1,400 and £1,500.

  • 4th frame: MR = £1,400 − £1,200 = £200; MC = £660 − £540 = £120. It adds £80, so make it.
  • 5th frame: MR = £1,500 − £1,400 = £100; MC = £840 − £660 = £180. It adds −£80, so don't.

Profit is maximised at 4 frames, priced at £350.

(b) TR − TC = £1,400 − £660 = £740. AC = £660 ÷ 4 = £165, so (AR − AC) × Q = (£350 − £165) × 4 = £740.

(c) Revenue maximiser: TR peaks at £1,500 at 5 frames, and the 6th would cut it (MR = £1,440 − £1,500 = −£60), so it charges £300. Sales maximiser: at 7 frames AC = £1,330 ÷ 7 = £190 = AR, so it charges £190 and just breaks even.

(d) At 3 frames profit per unit is £400 − £180 = £220, against £185 at 4. But total profit is £660 at 3 and £740 at 4: the 4th frame lowers profit per unit yet still adds £80. Always compare MR with MC for the next unit.

cards.front: Sketch the profit-maximising position of a firm with a downward-sloping demand curve. How do the price and output of a profit maximiser, a revenue maximiser and a sales maximiser differ?
cards.back:
The firm produces Q, where MC = MR, and reads the price P off the demand curve (D=AR). Average cost at Q is C, so profit per unit is P − C, and total profit is (P − C) × Q.

  • Profit maximisation: produce where MC = MR → the highest price and the lowest output of the three → the most profit for the owners.
  • Revenue maximisation: keep selling while each unit still adds revenue, so produce where MR = 0 → a lower price and more output → less profit, but a bigger business, which may suit managers paid on sales.
  • Sales maximisation: sell as much as possible without making a loss, so produce where AR = AC → the lowest price and highest output → only normal profit, but more market share.

A dot marks where MC crosses MR, at output Q. Dashed lines from Q go up to average cost C on the AC curve and price P on the demand curve

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how do satisficing, growth, survival and ethical aims each affect the price a firm charges? What decides which objective it follows?
cards.back:
• Satisficing: aiming for enough profit to keep the owners content → managers have room to pursue their own aims → price and output usually sit between the profit- and sales-maximising levels.
  • Growth or market share: a low starting price wins customers from rivals → sales and market share rise → profit is lower now, in the hope of more later.
  • Survival: in a downturn the firm cuts prices to keep cash coming in → as long as price covers variable cost, each sale still makes a contribution to fixed costs.
  • Ethical or social aims: paying suppliers a fair price raises costs → the firm charges more, relying on customers who value its stance.

Which objective, and so which price, depends on:

  • Who runs it: owners usually want profit, while managers may prefer growth in sales, which brings them status and pay.
  • Competition: a firm with close rivals has little room to price for anything but survival or market share.
  • Its stage: a new firm may chase sales to get known, then switch to profit once it is established.

cards.front: Define productive efficiency and allocative efficiency. How do they differ, and which market structures achieve them?
cards.back:
Productive efficiency — producing at the lowest possible average cost, where MC = AC.

Allocative efficiency — producing the combination of goods and services that consumers value most, so society's welfare is maximised, where price equals marginal cost (P = MC).

Productive efficiency is about how things are made: no resources wasted, so each unit costs as little as possible. Allocative efficiency is about what is made. A factory making a product nobody wants at the lowest possible cost is productively efficient, but the resources would have been better used on something else.

  • Perfect competition: in the long run, a firm achieves both.
  • Market power: a firm usually achieves neither. It sets a price above marginal cost and produces less than the lowest-cost output.

cards.front: What does it mean to decide at the margin? Build the chains: why is P = MC a trade-off between opportunity costs?
cards.back:
Firms and consumers rarely decide whether to make or buy anything at all. They decide whether to make or buy one more. That is thinking at the margin.

Every extra unit has an opportunity cost: the materials and labour it uses could have made something else. Marginal cost measures that cost, and the price measures how much consumers value the extra unit.

  • Price above MC: consumers value one more unit more than the resources it uses → society gains by producing more of it.
  • Price below MC: the resources are worth more elsewhere → society gains by producing less and moving them to another use.

Allocative efficiency is the point where no such gain is left: producing more of one good would mean giving up something consumers value more.

cards.front: Define productivity. Build the chains for the three ways the spec names to raise it and cut average cost. What limits the gain?
cards.back:
Productivity — output per unit of input in a given time period.

If workers produce more in the same time, the wage bill and other costs are spread over more units, so average cost falls.

  • Technology: a print shop buys a faster press → more jobs printed per hour by the same staff → lower labour cost per job → lower average cost.
  • Human capital: skills training and education → staff work faster and make fewer mistakes → less waste and rework → lower average cost.
  • Quality of management: better planning of rotas, stock and workflow → less time idle or waiting → more output from the same inputs → lower average cost.

Lower average cost lets the firm cut prices to win sales, or keep them and earn a higher margin. Either way it becomes more competitive.

The gain depends on: cost and time lags, as machinery and training cost money up front; staff, who may resist new technology if they fear for their jobs; and demand, as lower average cost only helps if the extra output can be sold.

cards.front: Define market orientation and contrast it with product orientation. How does it link to allocative efficiency, and what are its limits?
cards.back:
Market orientation — a business finds out what consumers want first, then designs and produces to match.

The opposite is product orientation, where a firm makes what it is good at and then looks for buyers. A market-oriented snack maker might test new flavours with shoppers before deciding which to launch.

Market orientation is allocative efficiency at the level of one firm:

  • The firm: production matches what customers want → less unsold stock and fewer discounts → higher sales and profit.
  • Consumers: the products they want are available → more satisfaction for the money they spend.

Limits: market research is expensive, and tastes can shift before production catches up.

cards.front: The price of petrol rises sharply. Trace the effects into a complement, a substitute and a labour market. What decides how big each knock-on effect is?
cards.back:
• Drivers: the cost of each car journey rises → people make fewer of them.
  • A complement: fewer car journeys → lower demand for town-centre car parks and motorway service stations → lower sales and profit there.
  • A substitute: more people take the bus or train → demand for bus and rail travel rises → higher revenue and profit for those firms.
  • A labour market: bus firms run more services → demand for bus drivers rises → their wages rise.

No market works alone. A change in one spreads to others through the goods consumers buy together or instead of each other, and through the materials and labour firms use. This is how the price mechanism moves resources between markets.

The size of each effect depends on how close the link is: a close substitute, or a firm that relies on one input, feels it far more than a distant one.

cards.front: Define collusion and a cartel. How does overt collusion differ from tacit collusion, and what does either do to consumers and to the colluding firms?
cards.back:
Collusion — firms cooperating instead of competing, for example to fix prices, share out customers or limit output.

Cartel — a group of firms with a formal agreement to collude. Cartels are illegal in the UK, and people found guilty of cartel activity can go to prison.

Collusion is most likely in an oligopoly, where a few firms can watch each other.

  • Overt collusion: firms openly agree, through meetings, messages or contracts. A cartel is overt collusion. The agreement leaves evidence, so it can be proven in court and punished.
  • Tacit collusion: firms coordinate without ever communicating, for example by following a price leader or never starting a price war. The result can be the same as a cartel's, but with no agreement to point to it is much harder to prove.

Either form:

  • Consumers: the firms act together like one monopoly → prices rise and output falls → consumers pay more and some are priced out.
  • The colluding firms: no price competition → higher margins → supernormal profit, but a risk of heavy fines if caught.

cards.front: Define restrictive practices and give four examples. Build the chain from a restrictive practice to its effect on consumers.
cards.back:
Restrictive practices — actions by a firm that limit competition, either against rivals or against the firms it trades with.

  • Predatory pricing: pricing below cost until a rival leaves the market, then raising prices.
  • Exclusive dealing: making retailers stock only the firm's own products.
  • Tying: selling one product only to customers who also buy another.
  • Refusal to supply: cutting off shops that also stock a rival's goods.

The chain: the practice keeps rivals out or pushes them out → fewer firms compete → the dominant firm can raise its prices later → consumers pay more and have less choice.

Competition law bans these practices when a dominant firm uses them.

cards.front: Define monopsony and a trade union. How does a dominant buyer affect its suppliers and consumers? How does a monopsony employer affect wages and jobs, and what can a trade union do about it?
cards.back:
Monopsony — a market with a single buyer, or one dominant buyer, of a good, service or factor of production.

Trade union — an organisation of workers that bargains with employers over pay and conditions.

A dominant buyer, such as a large car maker buying parts from small suppliers who have nowhere else to sell:

  • Suppliers: the buyer pushes down the price it pays → suppliers' margins shrink → smaller suppliers may go out of business or cut investment.
  • Consumers: the buyer's costs fall → it may pass some of the saving on as lower prices, or keep it as profit.

A monopsony employer, the one large employer in a town: workers have few other jobs to go to → it can pay less than a competitive market would → lower wages → fewer people take the jobs, so employment is lower too.

A trade union can threaten strikes to push wages above the competitive level → labour costs rise → firms may hire fewer workers or raise prices. Against a monopsony employer, though, it can push the wage back up towards the competitive level, raising pay and jobs together.

cards.front: Define a natural monopoly and say why one can arise. Sketch the diagram and compare the output, price and profit of a privatised, profit-maximising firm with those of a nationalised one. What is the market failure?
cards.back:
Natural monopoly — a market where one firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than two or more firms could.

Why: fixed costs are huge and the cost of serving one more customer is small. Two firms each laying gas pipes along every street would double the cost for no gain. Average cost keeps falling across the whole market, so one firm is the efficient outcome.

The diagram: LRAC is still falling where it meets D=AR, with LRMC below it.

  • Privatised firm: it maximises profit where MR = LRMC → output Qp at price Pp, with average cost Cp. Pp is above Cp, so it makes a profit.
  • Nationalised firm: it produces where LRMC meets D=AR → a larger output Qn at a lower price Pn. But Pn is below its average cost Cn, so it makes a loss.

The market failure: the one firm faces no competition. Left alone, it could charge high prices and let its service slip, so natural monopolies are regulated or publicly owned.

D=AR slopes down and cuts LRAC while LRAC is still falling, and MR is twice as steep, ending below the quantity axis. The privatised firm produces Qp, where MR meets LRMC, at price Pp on D=AR with average cost Cp on LRAC, below Pp. The nationalised firm produces the larger output Qn, where LRMC meets D=AR, at the lower price Pn, with average cost Cn above Pn

cards.front: Define market failure and explain why market power causes it. Evaluate the effects on economic agents and the government: what decides how serious the failure is?
cards.back:
Market failure — when the free market leads to too much or too little of a good being produced or consumed, so resources are not allocated in the best way for society.

Why market power causes it: a firm with little competition can raise its price above marginal cost and supply less → resources are under-allocated to the good → allocative inefficiency.

  • Consumers: higher prices and less choice → lower real incomes and less consumer surplus.
  • Workers: a monopsony employer pays less → lower living standards and less spending in the local economy.
  • Suppliers and small firms: squeezed by a dominant buyer or kept out by restrictive practices → lower profits, less investment and some closures.
  • Firms with power: supernormal profit → higher returns for owners, and funds for investment.
  • The government: it has to fund competition authorities and regulators → less to spend elsewhere, and it may pay more for services it buys from a dominant supplier.

How serious it is depends on: economies of scale, since a large firm's costs may be low enough that prices are no higher than with many small firms; the use of profit, since research and new products can benefit consumers over time; contestability, since the threat of entry limits price rises; and regulation, which can correct much of the failure, at a cost.

Judgement: name the type of market power first, because the fix differs. Breaking up a cartel would not raise costs, but breaking up a natural monopoly would.

cards.front: Define privatisation. What does it aim to achieve, and what is the risk when the business privatised is a natural monopoly?
cards.back:
Privatisation — transferring a business from public ownership to private ownership, usually by selling shares.

BT, British Gas and Royal Mail are UK examples. The aim is to bring in the profit motive and, where possible, competition.

  • Efficiency: private owners want profit → managers cut waste and costs → lower prices or better service for customers.
  • Government finances: the sale raises money once → the state no longer covers the business's losses.

The risk: a privatised natural monopoly is still a monopoly. Without competition, the profit motive can push prices up and quality down. That is why such firms are controlled by an industry regulator.

cards.front: Define the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). What are its main jobs, and how does it control mergers? How does EU competition policy still affect UK firms?
cards.back:
Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) — the UK government body that enforces competition and consumer law.

  • Review mergers, and block or change harmful ones.
  • Investigate and fine cartels and abuse of dominance.
  • Study whole markets that seem not to be working, and order changes.
  • Enforce consumer protection law.

Competition law bans agreements between firms that restrict competition, such as price fixing, and a dominant firm abusing its position, such as through predatory pricing. Firms can be fined, and individuals in a cartel can go to prison.

Mergers: a merger between rivals removes a competitor. The CMA can review one where the business being bought has UK turnover above £100 million, or where the merged firm would supply at least 25% of a product in the UK. If the deal would substantially lessen competition, it can block it, or approve it only if the firms sell off parts of the business.

EU competition policy: since Brexit it no longer applies inside the UK. But a UK firm whose cartel or abuse of dominance affects EU markets can be fined by the European Commission, and a global merger can need approval from both the CMA and the Commission → more cost and delay, and a risk the two decide differently.

cards.front:
A regulator caps the bills of the one firm that owns a region's water network at RPI − X, with X = 2%. Last year the average bill was £500, and RPI inflation is 5%.

(a) What is the highest the average bill can be this year? (b) The firm cuts its costs by more than the regulator expected. Who keeps the gain, and why does this give the firm an incentive to cut costs? (c) Why does the regulator also set quality targets, and what can stop the cap working?
cards.back:
(a) The bill may rise by no more than 5% − 2% = 3%. £500 × 1.03 = £515.

(b) The firm keeps any profit from beating X → the more it cuts its costs, the more profit it makes → it has an incentive to cut costs.

(c) Under a price cap, the firm could still raise profit by letting its service slip. Fines for missing targets, such as on supply cuts or complaints, stop that.

What can stop it working:

  • Information: the firm knows its costs far better than the regulator, so X may be set too low.
  • Regulatory capture: a regulator that grows too close to the firms it oversees may start to serve their interests.

cards.front: Why does the law protect consumers? Outline what UK consumer law requires, and build the chains for its effects on consumers and on firms.
cards.back:
Why: consumers know less about a product than the firm selling it, so the law sets minimum standards.

  • Consumer Rights Act 2015: goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described. If they are not, buyers can claim a refund, repair or replacement.
  • Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024: bans fake reviews and drip pricing, where extra charges appear only late in the buying process. The CMA can now decide for itself that a firm has broken consumer law, and fine it up to 10% of its global turnover.

The chains:

  • Consumers: clear prices and honest reviews → they can compare offers properly → better choices and fewer bad buys.
  • Firms: compliance costs money → but honest firms no longer lose sales to rivals who mislead.

cards.front: Why does the law protect employees? Name four UK protections, build the chains for their effects on workers and on firms, and say what the overall effect depends on.
cards.back:
Why: workers usually have less bargaining power than their employer, especially where it is a monopsony, so UK law sets minimum standards.

  • The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage: a legal floor on hourly pay.
  • The Equality Act 2010: bans discrimination on grounds such as sex, race, disability and age.
  • Health and safety law: makes employers manage risks at work.
  • Limits on working time and protection from unfair dismissal.

The chains:

  • Workers: higher minimum pay and safer conditions → higher real incomes and better wellbeing.
  • Firms: higher labour and admin costs → lower margins or higher prices, though better-treated staff may stay longer and work harder.

It depends on: firm size, since the paperwork weighs more heavily on a small business than a large one; and the labour market, since where employers have monopsony power, a minimum wage can raise pay without cutting jobs.

cards.front: Define regulatory capture. Why does it happen, and what does it do? Name the two other common reasons regulation fails.
cards.back:
Regulatory capture — when a regulator comes to serve the interests of the firms it regulates instead of the public.

When regulation makes things worse, that is government failure.

  • Why capture happens: the regulator relies on the firms for information, and staff often move between the two.
  • What it does: a captured regulator sets lenient price caps and weak targets → firms keep high prices and profits → consumers lose out.

The other two causes:

  • Poor information: the firm knows its own costs better than the regulator → caps and targets are set at the wrong level.
  • Unintended consequences: a firm meets the letter of a rule but not its purpose. An energy network with a target to answer complaints within a day might send a quick standard reply without fixing the problem.

cards.front: Build the chains for five benefits of regulating business.
cards.back:
• Lower prices: price caps and competition law stop firms exploiting market power → consumers pay less and buy more.
  • Safety and quality: minimum standards → consumers can trust what they buy without checking every detail.
  • Fair competition: the same rules for every firm → honest firms don't lose out to rivals who cut corners.
  • Protected workers: minimum pay and safe conditions → higher living standards and fewer injuries.
  • Wider society: rules on pollution and safety → less harm to people outside the market.

Each benefit comes with a cost to someone, so pair each one with a cost when you evaluate.

cards.front: Build the chains for five costs of regulating business.
cards.back:
• Compliance costs: paperwork, inspections and new equipment → higher costs → higher prices or lower profit.
  • A barrier to entry: rules cost a small firm as much as a large one → fewer new firms → less competition.
  • Less investment and innovation: a tight price cap leaves less profit → less spent on new products or upgrades.
  • Fewer jobs: higher labour costs → some firms hire fewer staff or automate.
  • Cost to taxpayers: regulators and enforcement have to be paid for → less to spend elsewhere.

cards.front: Evaluate: do the benefits of regulating business outweigh its costs?
cards.back:
Regulation corrects market failure, but it is not free: lower prices, safer products and fairer competition come with compliance costs, a higher barrier to entry and possibly less investment.

Whether the benefits outweigh the costs depends on:

  • The size of the market failure: a monopoly over an essential service, such as an energy network, justifies more regulation than a minor problem in a competitive market.
  • How the rules are designed: simple, targeted rules cost less to follow than broad ones.
  • The regulator's independence: a regulator free from capture and political pressure is more likely to protect consumers.
  • Firm size: large firms can absorb compliance costs that may force a small business to close.

Judgement: regulation is rarely good or bad for everyone, so name who gains and who pays. A price cap helps consumers now but may cost them later if investment falls. Weigh the two sides for the stakeholder the question asks about, and say which matters more in the case given.

cards.front:
A regulator oversees the one firm that owns a region's broadband network. It plans to cut the firm's price cap sharply, and to fine it whenever a fault takes more than two days to fix.

Analyse the likely effects on (a) households now, (b) households later and (c) the firm. (d) How could the plan fail?
cards.back:
(a) Households now: the cap stops the firm exploiting its market power → lower prices. The target → faults fixed faster → better quality.

(b) Households later: a tight cap leaves less profit → less spent on upgrades → the network may fall behind, so households could lose out over time.

(c) The firm: lower prices and the cost of meeting the target → lower profit. Paying for more repairs and the reporting the regulator asks for adds compliance costs.

(d) How it could fail:

  • Poor information: the firm knows its costs better than the regulator, so the cap may be set at the wrong level.
  • Unintended consequences: the firm could meet the letter of the target but not its purpose, for example by closing a hard fault and logging it again as a new one.
  • Regulatory capture: if the regulator grows too close to the firm, the cap and target may be set leniently.

Judgement: households gain now. Whether they gain overall depends on how far investment falls.

cards.front: Define a merit good and a public good. Why does the free market provide too little of each?
cards.back:
Merit good — a good or service with positive externalities in its consumption or production, so it is under-provided by the free market. Education, healthcare and vaccinations are examples.

Why too little: buyers count only their private benefit and ignore the external benefit to others → they consume less than the social optimum. Many also underestimate the private benefit itself.

Consequences: individuals gain fewer skills and lower lifetime earnings; firms get a less skilled, less healthy workforce and higher costs per unit; the government pays for more costly NHS treatment when poor health is caught late.

Public good — a good that is non-excludable, so non-payers cannot be stopped from using it, and non-rival, so one person's use does not reduce what is left for others. Street lighting and flood defences are examples.

Why little or none: nobody can be made to pay → people wait for someone else to buy it, the free rider problem → firms cannot make a profit → the market provides little or none of the good, even though society values it.

cards.front: Define a demerit good. Sketch the diagram for its over-consumption, marking the market outcome, the social optimum and the welfare loss. Who bears the consequences?
cards.back:
Demerit good — a good or service with negative externalities in its consumption or production, so it is over-provided by the free market. Cigarettes, alcohol and gambling are examples.

Why too much: buyers count only their private cost and ignore the harm to others. Many also underestimate the harm to themselves.

The diagram: MSB lies below D=MPB. Supply is S=MPC=MSC.

  • Market: where D=MPB meets supply, at P1 and Q1.
  • Social optimum: where MSB meets supply, at P2 and Q2. Q1 is more than Q2, so there is over-consumption.
  • Welfare loss: the shaded triangle between Q2 and Q1. Each of those units costs more to supply than it is worth to society.

Consequences:

  • Individuals: ill health → lost earnings and a lower quality of life.
  • Firms: staff off sick → lost output and cover costs → lower productivity.
  • The government: more treatment and policing → higher spending on the NHS and services.

The market equilibrium is at P1 and Q1, where supply meets D=MPB. The social optimum is at P2 and Q2, where supply meets MSB, with Q2 less than Q1 and P2 below P1. A shaded triangle between Q2 and Q1, between the supply curve and MSB, is the welfare loss

cards.front: Define factor immobility. Name its two types for labour, and explain why it is a market failure.
cards.back:
Factor immobility — when factors of production, such as labour and capital, cannot move easily between different uses or locations.

  • Occupational immobility: workers lack the skills for the jobs on offer. A steelworker cannot simply become an accountant.
  • Geographical immobility: workers cannot move to where the jobs are, because of housing costs, family ties or not knowing about vacancies elsewhere.

Why it is a market failure: the market does not clear. One region has unemployed workers while firms elsewhere cannot fill vacancies → those firms raise wages or turn down orders → higher costs and lost output. Meanwhile unemployment stays high where the jobs have gone.

cards.front: Define imperfect information and asymmetric information. How does each lead to market failure?
cards.back:
Imperfect information — when buyers or sellers lack the information they need to make the best decision.

Asymmetric information — when one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other.

  • Imperfect information makes merit and demerit goods worse: people misjudge their own costs and benefits → too little of merit goods is consumed and too much of demerit goods.
  • Asymmetric information lets the better-informed side take advantage. A landlord knows about damp that a new tenant cannot see, and a mechanic knows whether a repair is really needed.
  • Buyers who fear being misled may stop buying altogether → even good products go unsold.

cards.front: Why does the free market produce too much pollution and too many greenhouse gas emissions? Build the chains for the consequences of climate change, and evaluate what decides how serious they are.
cards.back:
Why too much: pollution and emissions are external costs, so the market produces too much of them. The damage builds up over time and falls on people far away and on future generations, who play no part in the market.

  • Firms: more floods, droughts and heatwaves → damaged property and disrupted supply chains → higher costs and insurance premiums.
  • Farming: less reliable harvests → more volatile food prices → lower real incomes for households.
  • Some industries gain: demand for renewable energy, insulation and flood defences rises → new investment and jobs.
  • The government: flood defences, disaster relief and health costs → higher public spending.

How serious it is depends on: time, since much of the damage comes decades after the emissions and is easy to ignore now; location, since coastal and farming regions are hit far harder than others; and action by other countries, since emissions affect the whole planet, so one country cutting back achieves little alone.

Judgement: not everyone loses, since some industries gain. But the largest costs fall far away and in the future, on people with no part in today's market, which is why the market leaves them out.

cards.front: Define internalising an externality. On a diagram for a good whose price leaves out an external cost, show what happens to price, output and the welfare loss when the externality is internalised.
cards.back:
Internalising an externality — making the producer or consumer pay for the external cost, so it becomes part of their private cost and the price.

The diagram: MSC lies above S=MPC, and the gap between them is the external cost of each unit. Demand is D=MPB=MSB.

  • Price leaves out the external cost: the market charges P1 and produces Q1, where S=MPC meets demand. Q1 is above the social optimum Q2, and the shaded triangle is the welfare loss.
  • Externality internalised: the price now covers the full social cost → it rises to P2 → output falls to Q2, where MSC meets demand → the welfare loss is removed.

Example: an airline's fares cover fuel, staff and aircraft, but not the damage done by the carbon its flights release.

The social optimum is at P2 and Q2, where MSC meets demand, with Q2 less than Q1 and P2 above P1. A shaded triangle between Q2 and Q1, between MSC and demand, is the welfare loss

cards.front: A firm's price covers only its private costs and leaves out an external cost. Build the chains for the four effects on society.
cards.back:
• Over-production: the price is too low → demand is higher than it should be → output goes above the social optimum → a welfare loss to society.
  • Third parties pay: the cost of the damage falls on people outside the market → through worse health, flood damage or clean-up bills → lower real incomes for people who gained nothing from the sale.
  • Clean firms lose out: the polluting firm's costs look lower than a clean rival's → it can charge less → the clean firm loses sales and has less reason to invest.
  • Wrong signals for investment: polluting methods stay cheap → firms keep using them → too little is spent on cleaner technology.

The reverse: if buyers pay only for their private benefit, goods with external benefits are under-consumed, and society misses out on gains it would value.

cards.front: Define an environmental externality. Give one external cost and one external benefit, and say whether the free market provides too much or too little of each.
cards.back:
Environmental externality — an external cost or benefit that affects the natural environment, such as air, water, land or the climate.

  • External cost: fertiliser washing off farmland into a river and harming its wildlife. The farm's prices leave out the damage → the market produces too much of its crops.
  • External benefit: a landowner planting trees, which take in carbon. Nobody pays the landowner for that gain → the market provides too little tree planting.

The market ignores both, because the people affected are not part of the deal and are not paid or charged for them.

cards.front: Why are environmental externalities harder to correct than most? Give four reasons.
cards.back:
• They are hard to measure: putting a money value on a lost wetland or cleaner air involves a lot of guesswork.
  • They cross borders: carbon emitted in one country warms the whole planet → no single government can fix it.
  • They build up over time: much of the cost falls on future generations → who have no say in today's market.
  • Nobody owns the environment: there is no owner to charge for its use → firms treat clean air and water as free.

Governments try to internalise these costs with policies such as taxes and tradable pollution permits.

cards.front:
For each, name who bears the external cost or misses out on the external benefit, and say why the price leaves it out:

  • a quarry whose blasting and dust affect the village next to it
  • a delivery firm whose diesel vans fill a busy high street with fumes
  • a household deciding whether to fit solar panels, which cut emissions from power stations.
cards.back:
• The quarry: villagers bear the noise, dust and cleaning bills. They are not part of the deal between the quarry and its buyers and are not compensated → the price of stone leaves out the damage → over-production.
  • The vans: people who live and shop on the street breathe the fumes. The firm pays for fuel and drivers, not for the harm to their health → too many van journeys.
  • Solar panels: the household counts only its own lower bills. Cutting emissions also helps everyone affected by climate change, including future generations, who pay nothing → too few panels are fitted: under-consumption.

On the diagram: for an external cost, the gap between MPC and MSC is the external cost of each unit, and the triangle is the welfare loss.

cards.front: Define tradable pollution permits. How does a permit scheme work, and what does it do to polluting firms, the environment and consumers?
cards.back:
Tradable pollution permits — permits, each allowing a set amount of pollution, that firms must hold to cover their emissions and can buy and sell.

How it works: the government sets a cap on total pollution and issues that many permits. A firm that cuts its emissions cheaply can sell its spare permits, and a firm that cannot must buy more. The cap is lowered over time. The UK Emissions Trading Scheme works this way for power stations, heavy industry and aviation.

  • Polluting firms: pollution now has a price → higher costs → an incentive to invest in cleaner methods.
  • The environment: the cap fixes total emissions → pollution falls as the cap tightens.
  • Consumers: firms pass on the cost → higher prices for energy and goods made with it.

cards.front:
Under a tradable permit scheme, a cement maker emits 1,000 tonnes of carbon a year but holds permits for only 800 tonnes. A permit for one tonne sells for £50, and the firm can cut its emissions at a cost of £30 a tonne.

(a) What would it cost to cover the gap by buying permits, and what would it cost to cut its emissions instead? Which does it choose? (b) If it could cut further at £30 a tonne, why would it keep cutting? (c) Why do total emissions not rise when another firm chooses to buy permits instead?
cards.back:
(a) The gap is 1,000 − 800 = 200 tonnes. Buying permits costs 200 × £50 = £10,000. Cutting costs 200 × £30 = £6,000. Cutting is £4,000 cheaper, so it cuts its emissions.

(b) Each further tonne it cuts costs £30 and frees a permit it can sell for £50 → a £20 gain on each tonne → pollution having a price gives it a reason to keep cutting.

(c) Every tonne emitted needs a permit, and the government issues only as many permits as the cap allows → a firm that buys permits uses ones another firm no longer needs → the cap fixes total emissions, and they fall as the cap is lowered.

cards.front: Build the chains: how do government provision and provision of information correct market failure? Give the cost or limit of each.
cards.back:
Government provision of public and merit goods, paid for through taxes. The market provides little or no public goods, such as national defence, so the state supplies them itself. Merit goods, such as vaccinations, are made free at the point of use, so cost does not stop anyone using them.

  • Consumers: a zero price → consumption rises towards the social optimum → a healthier, better-educated population. In the long term, a more skilled workforce brings higher productivity and tax revenue.
  • The cost: provision has to be paid for → higher taxes or borrowing, or less spent on something else.

Provision of information, such as health warnings, campaigns, or rules making firms publish information about what they sell, such as calories on the menus of large cafés, restaurants and takeaways in England.

  • Better information → consumers make choices closer to the social optimum → less over-consumption of demerit goods and more use of merit goods.
  • The limit: it is cheap, but people may ignore it, especially where a habit or addiction is involved. Attitudes shift only slowly, as with smoking.

cards.front: Evaluate policies to deal with market failure using the time frame. Give the short-term and long-term impact of an indirect tax, a subsidy, tradable permits, and legislation and regulation. What decides whether a policy works?
cards.back:
• Indirect tax: short term, higher prices, habits barely change where demand is price inelastic, and it hits poorer households hardest. Long term, people quit or switch, and firms change products, such as cutting sugar.
  • Subsidy: short term, higher government spending and more of the good bought. Long term, firms may come to rely on it, but the habit, such as better insulated homes, can last after it ends.
  • Tradable permits: short term, higher costs and prices for energy users. Long term, investment in clean technology, and emissions fall as the cap tightens.
  • Legislation and regulation: short term, harm is cut quickly, with compliance costs for firms. Long term, it can push firms to innovate, or drive trade to an illegal market.

Whether it works depends on:

  • PED: a tax cuts consumption only if demand is price elastic enough to respond.
  • Information: the government rarely knows the exact external cost, so taxes and caps may be set at the wrong level.
  • Time lags: new technology, skills and habits take years to change.
  • Who bears the cost: taxes on necessities, such as energy, take a larger share of poorer households' income.
  • Government failure: poorly designed policy can leave things worse than before.

Judgement: ask what the policy does in the first year and after ten. A permit scheme raises energy prices now but pays for cleaner technology later. Say which effect matters more in the case given.

cards.front:
Choose a policy for each market failure, and explain why it fits:

  • ships need a lighthouse on a dangerous stretch of coast, but no firm will build one
  • a chemical that factories release is found to cause serious harm to health
  • many power stations and steelworks emit carbon, and some can cut their emissions far more cheaply than others
  • people underestimate the long-term harm of heavy drinking.
cards.back:
• Lighthouse: government provision. It is a public good: no ship can be made to pay, so no firm can make a profit. The state provides it, paid for through taxes.
  • Chemical: legislation and regulation. A ban or an emissions limit works quickly and with certainty where the harm is serious. The costs are enforcement and higher compliance costs for firms.
  • Carbon: tradable pollution permits. The cap fixes total emissions. Firms that can cut cheaply do so and sell their spare permits, and the cap is lowered over time.
  • Heavy drinking: provision of information, such as health warnings and campaigns, so people choose closer to the social optimum. It is cheap but may be ignored where there is a habit or addiction. An indirect tax can add to it, but cuts drinking only if demand is price elastic enough to respond.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Define aggregate demand and state its formula. Sketch an increase in AD, and give four things that could cause it.
cards.back:
Aggregate demand (AD) — the total spending on an economy's goods and services at a given price level over a period of time: AD = C + I + G + (X − M).

The diagram: the price level goes up the side and real GDP along the bottom. AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2, so at the same price level PL, the real GDP demanded rises from Y1 to Y2. A change in the price level only moves the economy along the curve.

  • Interest rates fall: loans are cheaper and saving pays less → households spend more and firms invest more.
  • Confidence rises: households who feel their jobs are safe spend more, and firms expecting strong sales invest.
  • Fiscal policy loosens: the government spends more or cuts taxes.
  • Exports rise: a weaker pound or faster growth abroad → more overseas buyers for UK goods.

Each one reversed shifts AD to the left.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Define short-run aggregate supply and long-run aggregate supply. Sketch an increase in SRAS. What shifts SRAS, and what shifts LRAS?
cards.back:
Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) — the total output firms in an economy plan to supply at each price level in the short run, when the prices of factors of production, such as wages, are fixed.

Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) — the most an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed. It shows the economy's productive capacity.

The diagram: SRAS shifts right from SRAS1 to SRAS2, so at the same price level PL, the real GDP supplied rises from Y1 to Y2.

  • SRAS shifts with costs across the economy: lower wages, cheaper energy and raw materials, a stronger pound (cheaper imported inputs) or a cut in indirect taxes → firms supply more at each price level. A rise in any of them shifts SRAS left.
  • LRAS shifts with more or better resources: more workers, better skills, more capital, new technology → productive capacity grows. This is long-run economic growth, and it is what supply-side policies aim for.
cards.svgAlt: Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis. Two parallel upward-sloping lines, SRAS1 and SRAS2, with SRAS2 to the right and an arrow pointing right between them. A dashed line at price level PL meets SRAS1 above Y1 and SRAS2 above Y2, with Y2 greater than Y1

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Define full capacity output. Sketch the Keynesian LRAS curve and explain what happens to output and prices on each of its three sections. How does the classical view differ?
cards.back:
Full capacity output — the level of real GDP at which all of the economy's resources are in use, so output cannot rise any further in the short run.

The diagram: the Keynesian LRAS is flat at low real GDP, curves upwards as output rises, and becomes vertical at full capacity output, Yfe.

  • Flat: many workers and machines are idle → firms produce more without paying more for them → output rises with no rise in prices.
  • Rising: spare capacity runs out → firms bid for scarce workers and materials → output still rises, but costs and prices rise too.
  • Vertical: the economy is at Yfe → more spending only raises prices.

Classical view: LRAS is vertical at full capacity. The economy always returns there, so in the long run a change in AD moves only the price level. The Keynesian view is that the economy can stay below full capacity for a long time.
cards.svgAlt: Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis. The LRAS curve is horizontal at low real GDP, curves upwards more and more steeply as output rises, and becomes vertical at full capacity output, marked Yfe with a dashed vertical line

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Build the chains: what does each of these do to inflation and unemployment? (a) AD rises with spare capacity (b) AD rises near full capacity (c) AD falls (d) SRAS shifts left (e) LRAS shifts right. What does the effect depend on?
cards.back:
• (a) AD rises, spare capacity: more spending → firms bring idle workers and machines back into use → output rises with little change in prices → unemployment falls and inflation barely moves.
  • (b) AD rises near full capacity: firms compete for scarce staff and materials → wages and costs rise → prices rise with little extra output: demand-pull inflation.
  • (c) AD falls: households and firms spend less → firms cut output and need fewer workers → unemployment rises and inflation falls.
  • (d) SRAS shifts left: energy or wage costs rise → firms raise prices and cut output → cost-push inflation and higher unemployment at the same time.
  • (e) LRAS shifts right: productive capacity grows → output can rise without pushing up costs → growth with lower inflation, and more jobs if AD grows to match.

It depends on: spare capacity (the same rise in AD cuts unemployment in a recession but mainly causes inflation in a boom); the size of the shift, since the multiplier can make a small change larger; and time, since firms take time to hire, invest or raise prices.

Say where the economy starts before you shift a curve.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Define the multiplier effect. Why does an injection of spending raise real GDP by more than itself? State the formula, and give three things that make the multiplier larger.
cards.back:
Multiplier effect — the process by which an initial change in spending leads to a larger final change in real GDP.

Why: one person's spending is another's income. A council pays a firm to build a new sports centre → its workers spend part of their wages in local cafés → the café staff spend part of theirs. Each round is smaller, because some income leaks out as saving, tax or spending on imports.

  • MPC (marginal propensity to consume): the share of each extra pound spent on UK goods and services.
  • MPW (marginal propensity to withdraw): the share that leaks out, MPS + MPT + MPM. MPC + MPW = 1.

Larger when: leakages are small (low tax rates, little saving, few imports); there is spare capacity, so firms meet the extra demand with more output rather than higher prices; and confidence is high, so people spend extra income instead of saving it.

It works in reverse too: a fall in spending, such as fewer overseas orders for UK exporters, cuts incomes round after round.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front:
Out of each extra pound of income, households save 10p, pay 20p in tax and spend 20p on imports.

(a) Calculate the MPW, the MPC and the multiplier. (b) The government spends an extra £4 billion on new railway lines. By how much does real GDP rise? (c) Households grow worried about their jobs and now save 40p of each extra pound. What are the new multiplier and the new rise in real GDP, and why is it smaller?
cards.back:
• (a) MPW = 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.5. MPC = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5. Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.
  • (b) £4bn × 2 = £8 billion rise in real GDP.
  • (c) MPW = 0.4 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.8, so the multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25. £4bn × 1.25 = £5 billion. More of each pound leaks out as saving → less is spent again in each round → a smaller final rise in real GDP. Low confidence shrinks the multiplier.

The answer assumes spare capacity. Near full capacity, much of the extra spending goes into higher prices instead.
