cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: What does the AD/AS model show about the economy as a whole? Give three ways it helps, and evaluate its limits.
cards.back:
It puts the main objectives on one diagram: real GDP shows growth, the price level shows inflation, and the gap between output and full capacity shows unemployment.

  • Finding the cause: inflation with rising output points to strong demand; inflation with falling output points to a supply shock.
  • Choosing a policy: weak demand calls for demand-side policies; low capacity calls for supply-side policies.
  • Showing trade-offs: pushing AD up near full capacity buys a little growth at the cost of higher inflation.

Its limits: classical and Keynesian economists disagree about the shape of LRAS, so the same policy can look effective on one diagram and useless on the other. The model shows the direction of a change, not its size or timing. No one knows exactly where full capacity is.

Judgement: a rise in AD has a very different effect in a recession from in a boom. State whether there is spare capacity, using the evidence, then draw the shift on the matching part of the LRAS curve.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Define demand-side policies. Then define fiscal policy and monetary policy: who runs each, and what are its tools?
cards.back:
Demand-side policies — policies that change the level of aggregate demand (AD) to steer growth, unemployment and inflation.

Fiscal policy — changing the levels of government spending and taxation to affect aggregate demand.

  • Run by the government, through the Chancellor's Budget. Taxes are direct (on income and profit, such as income tax and corporation tax) or indirect (on spending, such as VAT and fuel duty).
  • Expansionary: more spending or lower taxes → AD shifts right. Contractionary is the opposite. Spending above tax revenue is a budget deficit, which the government borrows to cover.

Monetary policy — the use of interest rates and the money supply to influence aggregate demand, mainly to control inflation.

  • Run by the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, independently of the government, to keep CPI inflation at the government's 2% target.
  • Two tools: Bank Rate, which banks' own rates on loans, mortgages and savings follow, and quantitative easing.

The government does not set interest rates. Name the right body.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Define quantitative easing. When does the Bank of England use it, how does it raise AD, and what side effect can it have?
cards.back:
Quantitative easing (QE) — the central bank creating new money electronically and using it to buy assets, mostly government bonds, to increase the money supply.

When: Bank Rate is already close to zero, so it cannot be cut much further.

The chain: the Bank buys bonds from investors such as pension funds → bond prices rise and long-term interest rates fall → borrowing is cheaper for households and firms, and the sellers have money to lend or invest → spending and investment rise → AD shifts right.

Side effect: QE can push up house and share prices, which helps the people who own them.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Show expansionary demand-side policy on an AD/AS diagram for an economy with spare capacity. Name a policy that would encourage investment, one for jobs and one for growth. What happens to growth, jobs, prices and trade? How would the result differ at full capacity?
cards.back:
The diagram: on a Keynesian LRAS1, AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2, still below Yfe, and the price level rises from PL1 to PL2.

Policies: investment, a Bank Rate cut, QE or a cut in corporation tax; jobs, government spending on roads and housing; growth, an income tax cut.

  • Growth: more spending → firms raise output → real GDP rises, by more than the first injection because of the multiplier.
  • Jobs: firms need more staff → unemployment falls → household incomes rise.
  • Prices: as spare capacity runs out, firms compete for workers and materials → costs rise → demand-pull inflation.
  • Trade: higher incomes → more spending on imports → the current account deficit widens.

At full capacity (a classical vertical LRAS at Yfe), the same shift raises only the price level, and real GDP stays at Yfe.

Contractionary policy shifts AD left, and each chain runs the other way.
cards.svgAlt: Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis. A Keynesian LRAS1 curve is flat at low output, then rises, then becomes vertical at Yfe. AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2, with Y2 still below Yfe, and the price level rises from PL1 to PL2

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Build the chains for the policy conflicts and trade-offs of demand-side policy. Give five, and explain how fiscal and monetary policy can pull against each other.
cards.back:
• Growth or low inflation: boosting AD → more output and jobs → but near capacity, rising prices. Raising rates to cut inflation slows growth and can cost jobs.
  • Growth or the current account: higher incomes → more imports → a wider trade deficit.
  • Now or later: tax cuts and spending paid for by borrowing → more growth now → but higher debt interest, and higher taxes or lower spending in future.
  • Growth or equality: low interest rates and QE → higher house and share prices → gains for those who own them, while first-time buyers are priced out.
  • Growth or the environment: more output → more energy use and pollution.

Pulling against each other: if the government loosens fiscal policy while inflation is above target, the MPC may raise Bank Rate to offset it.

Policy-makers have to choose which objective matters most at the time.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Evaluate monetary policy against fiscal policy. Give the strengths and weaknesses of each, explain the time lags, and say what decides how well either policy works.
cards.back:
• Monetary policy, strengths: set by an independent MPC, free of short-term political pressure; Bank Rate can change at any meeting; a clear inflation target.
  • Monetary policy, weaknesses: long time lags; one rate for the whole country, so it cannot target a region or industry; little room to cut near zero, and QE can push up house and share prices.
  • Fiscal policy, strengths: can be aimed at a region, industry or income group; government spending adds to AD directly, and works when interest rates are already low.
  • Fiscal policy, weaknesses: slow to plan and pass; extra borrowing adds to the national debt; tax rises and spending cuts are unpopular, so politics can delay them.

Time lags: a change in Bank Rate takes around 18 to 24 months to work in full, partly because many mortgages are fixed. Fiscal policy waits for late data, a Budget and new law. A rate cut that arrives once recovery has started adds to inflation instead.

It depends on: confidence (worried households save a tax cut, firms won't borrow however cheap loans are); the size of the multiplier; spare capacity; and crowding out, where heavy government borrowing pushes up interest rates and private investment falls.

Judgement: against unemployment, either policy works only where it is caused by weak demand, not where people's skills don't match the jobs on offer. The MPC can decide at any meeting, but the full effect takes up to two years; fiscal policy is slower to agree, but can be aimed at the region or group worst hit. Say which matters more in the case given.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Define supply-side policies. Then define market-based and interventionist policies, with an example of each. Why are interventionist policies needed?
cards.back:
Supply-side policies — policies that aim to increase an economy's productive capacity, shifting long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) to the right.

Market-based policies — supply-side policies that reduce the government's role, so markets work more freely and incentives are stronger. Example: a cut in income tax, or deregulation.

Interventionist policies — supply-side policies in which the government spends, provides or directs resources to raise productive capacity. Example: spending on apprenticeships, or a new rail line.

  • Market-based policies rely on firms and workers responding to incentives.
  • Interventionist policies fill gaps the market leaves, because firms would provide too little of them, such as training workers who might leave for a rival firm.

Demand-side policy changes how much is spent. Supply-side policy changes how much the economy can produce. Many supply-side policies also cut firms' costs, so SRAS shifts right as well.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front:
Say whether each supply-side policy is market-based or interventionist, and name the aim it serves:

  • a cut in corporation tax
  • privatising a state-owned firm
  • funded childcare so parents can return to work
  • student loans
  • state spending on apprenticeships
  • faster planning approval for new building
  • government spending on broadband and power grids.
cards.back:
• Corporation tax cut: market-based; increase incentives, as firms keep more profit to invest.
  • Privatisation: market-based; promote competition.
  • Funded childcare: interventionist; reform the labour market.
  • Student loans: market-based; improve skills and the quality of labour, as people invest in their own skills.
  • Apprenticeships: interventionist; improve skills and the quality of labour.
  • Faster planning approval: market-based; improve infrastructure.
  • Broadband and power grids: interventionist; improve infrastructure.

The test: does it reduce the government's role and rely on incentives (market-based), or does the government spend, provide or direct resources (interventionist)?

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Build the chains: how does each of the five supply-side aims raise productive capacity? Increase incentives, promote competition, reform the labour market, improve skills, improve infrastructure.
cards.back:
• Incentives: lower tax on income → work pays more → more people join the labour force or work longer hours → more labour, so higher output.
  • Competition: lower barriers → new firms enter → existing firms must cut costs and innovate → lower prices and higher productivity.
  • Labour market: wages and hiring respond more easily to demand → firms take on staff more readily → lower unemployment.
  • Skills: better training → workers produce more per hour → firms' unit costs fall and workers can earn higher wages.
  • Infrastructure: faster transport and broadband → lower costs of moving goods and people → firms reach more customers and invest where they could not before.

Each one raises the quantity or productivity of labour and capital, so LRAS shifts right.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Show a successful supply-side policy on a Keynesian AD/AS diagram. What happens to real GDP and the price level, and how does the classical diagram show it? Why might AD move before LRAS?
cards.back:
The diagram: the whole Keynesian LRAS curve shifts right, from LRAS1 to LRAS2, so the economy reaches full capacity at a higher output. With AD unchanged, real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from PL1 to PL2.

Classical view: LRAS is vertical, so full capacity output itself moves, from Yfe1 to Yfe2. Real GDP rises and the price level falls.

AD first: many supply-side policies are government spending. Building a new motorway adds to G, so AD rises at once, while LRAS moves only once the road is open. Show both shifts, say which comes first, and use the gap between them as the time lag.
cards.svgAlt: Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping AD curve crosses a Keynesian LRAS1 curve, flat at low output and rising steeply to become vertical, at real GDP Y1 and price level PL1. LRAS shifts right to LRAS2, and AD now crosses it at the higher output Y2 and the lower price level PL2

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Evaluate supply-side policies. Give their strengths and weaknesses, the trade-offs they bring, and what decides how well they work.
cards.back:
• Strengths: growth without inflation, as capacity rises; lower structural unemployment, which demand-side policy cannot fix; exporters compete better on price as unit costs fall; more tax revenue and fewer benefit claims, so the budget deficit narrows over time.
  • Weaknesses: long time lags (a new apprentice takes years to become fully skilled); interventionist policies cost money, with an opportunity cost; uncertain results (a firm may keep a tax cut as profit); no help in a recession, since extra capacity is wasted if demand is weak.

Trade-offs: efficiency or equality (cuts to top tax rates, benefits and union power help higher earners most); the budget now or growth later; growth or the environment (new roads and runways); workers or firms (flexible contracts mean cheaper hiring but less job security).

It depends on: the type of policy (market-based is often cheaper for the government; interventionist can reach problems markets ignore); the cause of the problem (they help most where low output comes from a skills gap, poor transport or weak competition); and how well they are run, since money spent on the wrong projects is government failure.

Judgement: they suit a problem of capacity, not of weak demand, and their benefits arrive years later. Say what is holding output back before you recommend one.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front:
Give one effect on firms and one on individuals of each policy:

  • a higher Bank Rate
  • lower taxes
  • higher government spending
  • supply-side reform.
cards.back:
• Higher Bank Rate: firms face dearer loans and weaker sales, so they invest less, though firms with cash savings earn more. Individuals pay more on mortgages and loans, savers earn more, and prices rise more slowly.
  • Lower taxes: firms keep more profit after tax and sell more, so they invest more. Individuals have more take-home pay to spend, but public services may have less money.
  • Higher government spending: suppliers and builders win contracts, and firms gain customers as jobs are created. Individuals get more jobs and better services, but higher taxes or debt later.
  • Supply-side reform: better-trained staff and transport cut firms' costs, but new entrants bring more competition. Individuals gain skills and pay over time, but flexible contracts mean less job security.

The same policy can help one group and hurt another.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Compare the alternative approaches to macroeconomic policy: demand-side or supply-side, monetary or fiscal, market-based or interventionist. What does each choice trade off, and why do governments use a mix?
cards.back:
• Demand-side or supply-side: demand-side works within two years or so and suits a recession caused by weak spending. Supply-side takes years but raises capacity, so growth can last without inflation.
  • Monetary or fiscal: the MPC can change Bank Rate at any meeting, but it hits every region and industry alike. Fiscal policy can be aimed at a group, such as low-income households, but it is slower to agree and adds to borrowing.
  • Market-based or interventionist: tax cuts and deregulation cost the government less but can widen inequality. Spending on training and infrastructure fills gaps the market leaves but has a large opportunity cost.

A mix: demand-side policy to steady the economy now, and supply-side policy to raise its growth rate over time.

Judgement: each approach has a cost, so the best choice depends on the cause of the problem and how quickly it must be solved.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Set five criteria for success to judge whether a macroeconomic policy worked. Why does each one matter?
cards.back:
• Did it hit its target? Inflation back to 2%, unemployment down or growth up, measured against what the policy set out to do.
  • How quickly? A policy that works after the problem has passed has failed, even if the numbers improve.
  • At what cost? The money spent or tax revenue lost, and any damage to other objectives such as growth or the budget deficit.
  • Who gained and who lost? A policy that meets its target but hits low-income households hardest may not count as a success.
  • Did it last? A temporary boost is worth less than a lasting rise in capacity.

Decide what success would look like first, then judge the policy against it.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Build the chains for the five factors that decide how effective almost any macroeconomic policy is. What else can policy-makers not control?
cards.back:
• Time lags: monetary policy takes 18 to 24 months to work in full, and supply-side policy years → the economy may have changed by then.
  • The size of the multiplier: little of any extra income saved, taxed or spent on imports → a change in spending has a larger final effect.
  • Spare capacity: in a recession, extra demand raises output and jobs → near full capacity, it mostly raises prices.
  • Confidence: worried households and firms save rather than spend → a tax cut or rate cut does less.
  • Side effects: costs elsewhere, such as more borrowing or higher house prices, and responses no one intended, such as a firm banking a tax cut as profit instead of investing it.

Beyond their control: shocks such as a jump in world energy prices, and data that arrive late and are often revised.

cards.topic: 4.4 Macroeconomic Policies and Impact on Firms and Individuals
cards.front: Between late 2021 and 2023, the MPC raised Bank Rate from 0.1% to 5.25%. CPI inflation had peaked at 11.1% in 2022, driven largely by energy and food prices. Judge the policy against the criteria: target, time lags, the cause, and side effects. What did fiscal policy add?
cards.back:
• Target: inflation fell back to 2% in 2024, so by that test the policy succeeded.
  • Time lags: many homeowners were on fixed-rate mortgages and paid the higher rate only when their deal ended → the squeeze on spending built up over two years.
  • The cause: higher rates cannot lower world gas prices. They work by cutting demand at home → part of the fall in inflation came from energy prices falling back, not from the policy.
  • Side effects: higher repayments for borrowers and firms → less spending and investment → very slow growth in 2023.

Fiscal policy: the Energy Price Guarantee capped household energy prices, holding a typical bill at about £2,500 a year. It worked within weeks and protected low-income households, but was paid for with extra borrowing.

Judgement: the rate rises worked, but slowly, because most mortgages were fixed. Monetary policy tackled the inflation; fiscal policy eased its cost for households while it lasted.

cards.front:
Define risk and uncertainty, and explain why the difference matters to a firm.

Classify each as a risk or an uncertainty: (a) stock stolen from a shop; (b) whether a new flavour of crisps will sell; (c) a delivery van crashing; (d) customers' tastes moving away from the firm's product.
cards.back:
Risk — an unknown outcome whose chances can be measured, usually from past data, so a probability can be put on it.

Uncertainty — an unknown outcome whose chances cannot be measured, because there is no past record to go on.

  • Risk can be priced: it can be measured → an insurer or a bank can work out a fair charge for taking it on → the firm swaps an unknown loss for a known cost, such as an insurance premium.
  • Uncertainty cannot: no one can put a number on it → no one will sell cover against it → the owners carry it themselves. Profit is their reward for doing so.
  • (a) Risk: records across many shops show how often theft happens, so the stock can be insured.
  • (b) Uncertainty: a new product has no past record to go on.
  • (c) Risk: records across thousands of vans show roughly how many crash each year.
  • (d) Uncertainty: there is no past record of how tastes will change, so no insurer will cover it.

cards.front: Define an economic shock, and distinguish a demand shock from a supply shock. Build the chains for a negative shock of each kind, and give three things that decide how badly a firm is hurt.
cards.back:
Economic shock — an unexpected event that suddenly changes demand or costs across the economy.

A demand shock changes how much customers buy. A supply shock changes what it costs to produce. Few firms see either coming, so shocks are a source of uncertainty.

  • Demand shock: sales fall suddenly → revenue drops while rent and loan repayments stay the same → cash runs short → firms cut staff, delay investment or close.
  • Supply shock: energy or materials cost more → unit costs rise → the firm raises prices and loses sales, or holds prices and accepts a lower profit margin.
  • Workers and consumers: job losses and higher prices → lower real incomes → less spending, which passes the shock on to other firms.

Shocks also create winners: online retailers and delivery firms when shoppers move online, and energy producers when energy prices jump.

How badly a firm is hurt depends on:

  • Size and duration: a business can ride out a short shock on its savings. One that lasts years can change what customers buy for good.
  • Cash reserves and debt: a firm with cash in the bank and little borrowing can wait for demand to recover. A heavily borrowed firm may run out of cash first.
  • Ability to pass costs on: with price inelastic demand or a strong brand, a firm can raise prices after a supply shock and keep most of its sales.

cards.front: Define exchange rate risk and a forward contract. How does hedging help a firm that trades abroad, and what decides whether it is worth it?
cards.back:
Exchange rate risk — the risk that a change in the exchange rate alters the value of a payment a firm has agreed to make or receive in a foreign currency.

Forward contract — an agreement made today to buy or sell a currency on a set future date at an exchange rate fixed now.

  • An importer paying in dollars: if the pound weakens, it pays more pounds.
  • An exporter paid in euros: if the pound strengthens, it receives fewer pounds.

Banks sell forward contracts in the forward market. Using one to remove exchange rate risk is hedging: it fixes the pound value of a deal → the firm can set prices and budget, and a sudden currency move cannot wipe out its margin → it is more willing to sign overseas deals.

Whether it is worth it depends on:

  • Lost gains: the firm gives up any benefit from a favourable move.
  • Cost and scale: banks charge for the service, so a small firm with few overseas deals may not bother.
  • Known amounts and dates: a contract fixes one sum on one date. It cannot protect sales the firm has not yet won, or a fall in the pound that lasts for years.

cards.front:
A Scottish whisky distiller sells to a US importer for $390,000, to be paid in three months. Its bank offers a forward contract at £1 = $1.25.

(a) How many pounds does the contract fix the distiller's revenue at? (b) Without the contract, how many pounds would it receive if in three months the rate is £1 = $1.30, or £1 = $1.20? (c) In each case, did the contract help or cost the distiller, and by how much? Why might it hedge anyway?
cards.back:
• (a) $390,000 ÷ 1.25 = £312,000.
  • (b) At $1.30 (pound stronger): $390,000 ÷ 1.30 = £300,000. At $1.20 (pound weaker): $390,000 ÷ 1.20 = £325,000.
  • (c) Pound stronger: the contract gains it £12,000 (£312,000 against £300,000). Pound weaker: it receives £13,000 less than it would have without the contract (£312,000 against £325,000).

For an exporter, a stronger pound means fewer pounds when the dollars arrive: the reverse of an importer.

Why hedge anyway: either way, the distiller knows its revenue from the day it signs the deal, so it can set prices and budget with confidence. The price is giving up the gain from a weaker pound.

cards.front: Define insurance. How does pooling risk make it work, what three things does it do for a business, and what are its limits?
cards.back:
Insurance — a contract in which a firm pays a regular sum, the premium, and the insurer agrees to pay compensation if a specified loss happens.

Pooling risk: an insurer collects premiums from thousands of firms, knowing from past data that only a few will claim in a year. The premiums from the many pay for the losses of the few.

  • Survival: a flood ruins a print shop's presses → the insurer pays for new ones → the shop reopens instead of closing, and its staff keep their jobs.
  • Steady costs: a fixed premium replaces a large, unpredictable loss → cash flow is easier to forecast.
  • Access to finance: banks lending against property usually insist it is insured → insurance protects their collateral → the firm can borrow.

Its limits:

  • Only risks are covered: no insurer will pay out because sales fell, a rival undercut the firm or a product flopped. Those are uncertainties, and the firm must rely on something else, such as cash reserves.
  • Premiums are a cost: they rise after a claim or in high-risk areas, such as flood plains, and some firms insure for less than their assets are worth to save money.

Employers' liability insurance, which covers claims from injured staff, is required by law as soon as a firm takes on employees.

cards.front: Define the financial sector. Name the seven roles the spec gives it, with one line on what each does.
cards.back:
Financial sector — the banks, building societies, insurers, investment funds and markets that handle money for households, firms and the government.

  • Mobilising savings for lending: it pools many small savings so they can be lent in large amounts. Savers earn interest or a return, and one failed borrower is a small loss spread across thousands of savers.
  • Lending to business for working capital: overdrafts and short-term loans for working capital, and longer loans for machinery, buildings and technology.
  • Lending to individuals: mortgages, personal loans and credit cards let households buy now and pay over time.
  • Facilitating the exchange of goods and services: card payments, bank transfers and direct debits move money between buyers and sellers, so firms can sell to customers they will never meet, online and overseas.
  • Assessing creditor risk: deciding whether to lend, how much, and at what rate.
  • Forward markets in currencies and commodities: a firm agrees today the price at which it will buy or sell on a future date. A coffee chain can fix what it will pay for beans next year.
  • A market for equities: a stock exchange, where companies sell shares to raise money and investors trade them.

cards.front: Define working capital. Why does a profitable firm still need credit to run from day to day, and what happens to it when credit dries up?
cards.back:
Working capital — the money available for a business's day-to-day running, measured as current assets minus current liabilities. It pays for stock, staff and suppliers before customers pay.

A toy shop buys its Christmas stock in the autumn and pays its supplier straight away, but is paid by its customers only as the stock sells. An overdraft or short-term loan bridges the gap.

  • When credit flows: credit pays for stock and equipment → output and sales rise sooner → higher profit and more jobs. With longer-term loans for investment as well, a firm can grow faster than its own profits would allow.
  • When credit dries up: a profitable firm still has bills to pay before its customers pay it → it runs short of cash → it cuts orders or staff, or fails.

cards.front: Define creditor risk. How does a bank assess it, and why does it matter to the whole economy whether banks do this well, badly or too cautiously?
cards.back:
Creditor risk — the risk to a lender that a borrower does not repay what it owes.

Before lending, a bank checks the borrower's credit history, income or cash-flow forecast, and any collateral on offer. It then decides whether to lend, how much, and at what rate. Riskier borrowers pay more interest to cover the greater chance of default.

This decides where savings go:

  • Done well: money goes to borrowers likely to use it productively and repay → fewer bad debts → banks stay sound and keep lending.
  • Done badly: loans go to borrowers who cannot repay → defaults rise → banks make losses and cut lending to everyone, as in 2007-08.
  • Done too cautiously: new firms with no track record or collateral are turned down → good ideas go unfunded → less investment and enterprise.

cards.front: Define equities. Distinguish the primary market from the secondary market, and explain why the secondary market matters to a company that receives nothing from it.
cards.back:
Equities — shares in a company, each giving its owner part-ownership and a share of any profits paid out as dividends.

A stock exchange, such as the London Stock Exchange, does two jobs:

  • Primary market: a company first sells shares to the public → it raises new money for investment.
  • Secondary market: after that, investors buy and sell those shares between themselves.

Why the secondary market matters: investors know they can sell their shares whenever they want → they are more willing to buy in the first place → companies can raise large sums without taking on debt or paying interest.

cards.front: Evaluate the importance of the financial sector. How does it help firms, households and trade, and what decides how much it helps?
cards.back:
• Firms: savings are channelled into loans and share issues → firms can fund working capital and investment → higher output, productivity and jobs.
  • Households: mortgages and loans let them spread big purchases over time → consumption is steadier → firms' sales are steadier too. The risk is debt that grows faster than incomes: if rates rise or jobs are lost, repayments swallow more income and spending falls sharply.
  • Trade: fast payments and forward markets cut the cost and risk of buying and selling abroad → more trade and specialisation.

How much it helps depends on:

  • Who gets the credit: lending for houses and existing assets raises prices without adding to what the economy can produce. Lending to firms for investment does.
  • The size of firm: large companies can issue shares and bonds. Small firms depend on banks, and lose out first when banks become cautious.
  • How much risk the sector takes: too much lending to weak borrowers can end in a crisis that cuts credit to everyone. Regulation by the Bank of England tries to prevent this.

Judgement: the sector adds most when its credit goes to firms that invest, reaches small firms as well as large ones, and is lent without taking on too much risk.

cards.front: Define a central bank and Bank Rate. What are the Bank of England's two main aims, and why do the rest of the economy's interest rates follow Bank Rate?
cards.back:
Central bank — the bank that manages a country's currency and interest rates, and oversees its banking system. In the UK it is the Bank of England.

Bank Rate — the interest rate the Bank of England pays commercial banks on the money they keep with it overnight. It is also called the base rate or the official interest rate.

  • Monetary stability: low and steady inflation. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) handles it by setting Bank Rate, independently of the government.
  • Financial stability: a banking system that keeps working in bad times. The Financial Policy Committee (FPC) handles it.

Why other rates follow: if the Bank pays more on banks' deposits, they will only lend to households and firms at higher rates too → a change in Bank Rate soon changes rates on new mortgages, business loans, overdrafts and savings accounts.

cards.front: What inflation target does the MPC work to, and what happens if inflation misses it? Explain why the MPC sets Bank Rate for two years ahead, and evaluate how well Bank Rate controls inflation.
cards.back:
The target: 2% CPI inflation, set by the government. If inflation misses it by more than one percentage point either way, the Governor must write an open letter to the Chancellor explaining why and what the Bank will do.

The chain: inflation looks set to rise above target → the MPC raises Bank Rate → loan and mortgage repayments rise, saving pays more, and fewer projects are worth funding → aggregate demand falls → firms find it harder to raise prices and workers to win big pay rises → inflation slows.

Two years ahead: a change in Bank Rate takes around 18 to 24 months to have its full effect, so the MPC sets rates for where it expects inflation to be in two years, not where it is today.

How well it works depends on:

  • The cause of the inflation: higher rates reduce demand. They cannot make imported energy or food cheaper, so cost-push inflation is cut only by squeezing demand harder, at a cost to output and jobs.
  • Time lags: many homeowners have fixed-rate mortgages, so a rise reaches them only when their deal ends. A forecast that turns out wrong can leave rates too high for too long.
  • Credibility: if firms and workers believe the Bank will hit 2%, they set prices and pay claims accordingly, and inflation falls with smaller rate rises.

Judgement: Bank Rate works best when inflation comes from too much demand and the Bank is believed. Against inflation from imported energy or food, it works only at a cost to output and jobs.

cards.front: Define the Financial Policy Committee (FPC). How does its job differ from the PRA's and the FCA's, what are its three main tools, and what trade-off do tighter rules involve?
cards.back:
Financial Policy Committee (FPC) — the Bank of England committee that looks for risks to the financial system as a whole and acts to reduce them.

  • The FPC looks for systemic risk: problems, such as a lending boom, that could hit many banks at once.
  • The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), part of the Bank, supervises individual banks.
  • The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), separate from the Bank, checks that firms treat customers fairly.

The FPC's main tools:

  • Capital buffers: it can make banks hold extra capital, money from shareholders that absorbs losses, when risks are building. In a downturn it can release the buffer so banks keep lending.
  • Limits on risky mortgages: it caps the share of new mortgages lenders can make at 4.5 times or more a borrower's income. Such loans are allowed, but only as a limited part of new lending.
  • Stress tests: the Bank regularly checks whether the largest banks could survive a severe recession. Those that fall short must strengthen their finances.

The trade-off: the FPC raises the capital buffer → banks are safer but have less to lend → credit costs a little more → slightly less investment and spending. Looser rules risk the kind of lending boom that ended in 2007-08.

cards.front: Why is the Bank of England the banker to the banks? Define a lender of last resort, explain why even a sound bank can need one, and say what the case for it depends on.
cards.back:
Commercial banks hold accounts at the Bank of England, just as firms hold accounts at a high-street bank, and use them to settle payments with each other. That makes the Bank the banker to the banks.

Lender of last resort — a central bank lending to a commercial bank that is short of cash and cannot borrow anywhere else.

Why a sound bank can need one: a bank lends most of its deposits out for years, so it never has enough cash to repay every saver at once → if savers fear for the bank and all try to withdraw together, a bank run, even a sound bank can run out of cash.

  • Savers: the Bank of England lends → the commercial bank can pay out every withdrawal → panic subsides.
  • The wider economy: one bank's failure cannot spread to others it owes money to → banks keep lending to firms and households.

The case for it depends on:

  • Short of cash, or bust: the role is meant for banks with a cash shortage, not banks whose loans have gone bad. The Bank lends only against good collateral, and charges more than normal for it.
  • Moral hazard: if banks expect to be rescued, they may take bigger risks. That is why the lender of last resort comes with regulation from the FPC and PRA.

cards.front:
For each, say which Bank of England committee or which regulator is responsible, and why:

  • (a) CPI inflation is forecast to be 4% in two years' time
  • (b) lenders are making more and more mortgages at five times the borrower's income
  • (c) one bank's own finances look weak after a run of bad loans
  • (d) a lender is treating its customers unfairly
cards.back:
• (a) The MPC: it targets 2% CPI inflation and sets Bank Rate for where it expects inflation to be in two years, so it would raise Bank Rate.
  • (b) The FPC: a lending boom is a systemic risk. It can use its cap on the share of new mortgages made at 4.5 times income or more, and make banks hold a bigger capital buffer.
  • (c) The PRA: it supervises individual banks. The FPC looks at the system as a whole.
  • (d) The FCA: it checks that firms treat customers fairly, and is separate from the Bank of England.

Keep the two committees apart: the MPC targets inflation, and its tool is Bank Rate. The FPC targets the safety of the whole financial system, and its tools are rules on how banks lend and how much capital they hold.

cards.front: Define a sub-prime mortgage, speculation and a market bubble. How did the US house price bubble make sub-prime lending look safe, and why did the losses turn up in banks around the world when it burst?
cards.back:
Sub-prime mortgage — a home loan to a borrower with a poor credit record or low income, who is more likely than most to default.

Speculation — buying an asset mainly because you expect its price to rise, so you can sell it at a profit.

Market bubble — a rise in an asset's price far above what its underlying value can justify, driven by buyers expecting further rises.

  • Looking safe: house prices were rising → if a borrower could not pay, the house could be sold for more than the loan → banks and buyers kept betting that prices would keep rising.
  • Spreading: US lenders offered sub-prime loans with low starting rates, often with little check on income, then sold them on. Thousands of mortgages were bundled into securities and bought by banks worldwide.
  • Bursting: rates reset higher and prices fell → borrowers defaulted, and owed more than their homes were worth → lenders could not get their money back → losses turned up in banks far from the US, and no one knew exactly which banks held them.

cards.front: Define moral hazard and organisational culture. Use each to explain why banks took such large risks before the crisis, and why the cost was a negative externality.
cards.back:
Moral hazard — taking more risk because someone else will bear the cost if it goes wrong.

Organisational culture — the shared values and habits that shape how people in a business behave.

  • Too big to fail: the largest banks were so big, and so linked to the rest of the economy, that governments could not let them collapse → banks expected a rescue if bets went wrong → they took bigger risks for bigger profits, with thin capital to cover losses.
  • Culture: staff were paid large bonuses for selling loans and making short-term profit, and lost nothing personally when those loans failed later → warnings from risk managers were often ignored while profits were high. Lenders that sold mortgages on had little reason to check whether borrowers could repay.

A negative externality: when the banks failed, much of the cost fell on taxpayers and workers who had no part in the decisions.

cards.front: Define a credit crunch. Build the chain by which the banking crisis became a recession, then link the causes of the crisis into a single chain.
cards.back:
Credit crunch — a sudden, sharp fall in the amount banks are willing to lend.

Once banks were losing money, they hoarded cash to protect themselves.

  • Firms: banks cut overdrafts and refused new loans → firms could not fund stock, wages or investment → even profitable businesses cut output, laid off staff or failed.
  • The wider economy: less investment and more job losses → lower spending → lower sales for other firms → more loans go bad, and banks cut lending again.

Linking the causes: a culture of bonuses for lending, plus moral hazard → banks made sub-prime loans → a house price bubble made those loans look safe → when it burst, losses caused a credit crunch → that is what reached firms and workers.

cards.front: How did banking regulation contribute to the global financial crisis? Give four ways UK regulation has changed since, with the problem each targets, and evaluate how well the new rules work.
cards.back:
Before the crisis regulation was light. UK supervisors checked each bank on its own, and no one was responsible for spotting a risk building up across the whole system. Banks were allowed to run with little capital and to rely on short-term borrowing from each other, which vanished in 2007-08.

  • More capital and cash (Basel III): banks had too little to absorb losses or meet withdrawals.
  • New regulators (the FPC, PRA and FCA): no one watched the system as a whole.
  • Regular stress tests: banks were not tested against a severe recession.
  • Ring-fencing: risky investment banking could sink ordinary customers' deposits.

How well it works depends on:

  • The cost to lending: safer banks hold more capital → they lend less, or charge more → less investment and slower growth.
  • Risk moving elsewhere: tighter rules on banks can push lending to less regulated firms, such as investment funds, where the risk is harder to see.
  • Moral hazard remains: as long as a bank is too big to fail, it may still count on a rescue. Rules that make shareholders and lenders bear losses first try to change that.

Judgement: the new rules make banks safer, but at some cost to lending and growth, and they cannot fully remove the risk while some banks are still too big to fail.

cards.front: Build the chains for the impact of the financial crisis on households, firms, workers, savers and the government. Why was the impact uneven?
cards.back:
• Households: recession and job losses → lower incomes → some could not repay mortgages and lost their homes. Mortgages became harder to get, especially for first-time buyers.
  • Firms: the credit crunch cut their finance while demand was falling → lower sales and profit → investment cut and many businesses failed.
  • Workers: firms cut jobs → unemployment rose → those still in work had little bargaining power, so real wages fell for years.
  • Savers: the Bank of England cut Bank Rate to 0.5% and began quantitative easing → savings earned almost nothing for a decade.
  • Government: bank rescues, a temporary VAT cut to support spending, lower tax revenue and higher spending on benefits → a much bigger budget deficit → more borrowing → spending cuts and tax rises in the years that followed.

Why it was uneven:

  • Debt or savings: borrowers on variable-rate mortgages gained from low rates. People living on interest from savings lost.
  • Assets: low rates and QE pushed up the prices of shares and houses, which helped those who already owned them more than those trying to buy.
  • The industry: construction, car sales and other industries reliant on credit were hit hardest. Discount retailers gained as shoppers traded down.
